```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
```

## Why this matters

Exploratory analysis has a reputation as the polite preamble to the real work. Treat it
that way and it will cost you a paper.

A model will not tell you that your salinity column contains `-999`. It will fit
happily, report a plausible score, and hand you coefficients built on a mean salinity
of 2 PSU. Every problem in this section's dataset is visible in about ten minutes of
looking, and invisible in the model output afterwards.

The purpose of this pass is not to find results. It is to find out what is wrong.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

A workable order, roughly cheapest first:

1. **Shape and types** — how many rows, how many columns, what did the reader decide
   each column was?
2. **Missingness** — how much, in which columns, and *is it patterned*?
3. **One variable at a time** — range, distribution, impossible values, spikes.
4. **Categories** — every level, with counts. Not a sample: every level.
5. **Two variables at a time** — relationships, and correlations you did not expect.
6. **The response** — its distribution, and the balance of classes if it is categorical.
7. **By group** — does anything differ by vessel, observer, year, gear?

Step 7 is the one most often skipped, and the one that catches instrument drift.

## Worked example

```{r}
#| label: load
raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw()

dim(raw)
```

### Numeric ranges

The highest-yield ten seconds in all of data preparation: print the minimum and maximum
of every numeric column and read them as a scientist.

```{r}
#| label: ranges
raw |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric),
                   list(min = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        max = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "stat"), names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Three things there should stop you.

**Salinity has a minimum of $-999$ and a mean of 2.24.** No ocean is 2 PSU. This is the
sentinel-value trap: some instrument or export wrote `-999` to mean "missing", and
because it is a number, nothing complained. Temperature has it too.

**Depth reaches 1581 m** on a shelf survey whose stations were meant to be under 200 m.

**Chlorophyll has a minimum but the row count differs** — it contains real `NA`s, which
is the honest way to record a missing value.

### Seeing the sentinel

```{r}
#| label: fig-damage
#| fig-cap: "Left: all salinity values. The real ocean is the sliver at the right; everything at −999 is a missing value wearing a number's clothes. Right: chlorophyll is missing far more often in winter — missingness with a pattern, which is the kind that biases results."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. The left panel is a histogram of salinity with a tall bar at minus 999 and a narrow cluster of real values near 34, separated by a wide empty gap. The right panel is a bar chart of the percentage of missing chlorophyll by season: about 1 percent in autumn, 2 in spring, 4 in summer and 19 in winter."
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4
p_sentinel <- ggplot(raw, aes(salinity_psu)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = -999, y = 30, label = "−999\n(25 rows)", hjust = -0.15,
           colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Salinity (PSU)", y = "Stations",
       title = "A number that is not a measurement")

p_missing <- raw |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(missing = 100 * mean(is.na(chlorophyll_mg_m3))) |>
  mutate(season = fct_reorder(season, missing)) |>
  ggplot(aes(missing, season)) +
  geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(missing), "%")), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = "Chlorophyll missing (%)", y = NULL,
       title = "Missing, but not at random")

p_sentinel + p_missing
```

That left-hand panel is the whole argument for plotting before modelling. One
histogram, no statistics, and the problem is unmissable.

### Every category, with counts

```{r}
#| label: categories
raw |> count(substrate, sort = TRUE)
```

Four substrate types, twelve spellings. A model will treat `Sand`, `SAND`, `sand` and
`sandy` as four unrelated categories, splitting the evidence for sand four ways.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The file actually holds fourteen
Two of the original spellings had trailing spaces — `"mud "` and `"gravel "`. `readr`
trims whitespace by default, so they were silently repaired before you saw them. That
is convenient here and alarming in general: a different tool, or `trim_ws = FALSE`,
gives you fourteen categories instead of twelve. Know what your reader is fixing for
you.
:::

### The response

```{r}
#| label: response
raw |> count(rare_species) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

The rare species is present at 5% of stations. Remember this number: any classifier
you build for it must be compared against 95% accuracy, which you can get by answering
"absent" every time.

### By group

```{r}
#| label: by-vessel
raw |>
  filter(salinity_psu != -999) |>
  group_by(vessel) |>
  summarise(stations = n(),
            mean_salinity = round(mean(salinity_psu), 2),
            mean_temperature = round(mean(temperature_c[temperature_c != -999]), 2))
```

The two vessels differ by 0.42 PSU in mean salinity, with no matching temperature
difference. Two vessels sampling the same shelf should not disagree like that. This is
an instrument calibration offset, and it would have been invisible in every plot that
pooled the fleet.

## What the results mean

Ten minutes of looking produced six findings, each of which is a *decision* rather than
a repair:

| Finding | The decision it forces |
| --- | --- |
| `-999` in salinity and temperature | Convert to `NA` — then decide what to do about missing values |
| Depths up to 1581 m | Are these errors or real? Correct, drop, or flag |
| Twelve spellings of four substrates | Standardise — and check no genuine distinction is being merged away |
| Chlorophyll missing 19% in winter | Dropping those rows would delete most of winter |
| Rare species at 5% | Accuracy is the wrong metric before you have even started |
| One vessel reads 0.42 PSU high | Correct it, model it, or drop salinity entirely |

None of these is answered by a tool. Each needs someone who knows how the data was
collected, which is why exploratory analysis cannot be delegated to a package or an
assistant.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Exploring can itself leak
We have just looked at every row, and we will later hold some of them back as a test
set. Strictly, anything you learn here — that salinity needs fixing, that winter is
sparse — is information from the test set influencing your modelling choices.

This is unavoidable and mostly benign; you cannot clean data you are not allowed to
look at. Keep it benign by restricting this pass to *data quality* and keeping decisions
about the response, and any choice made by comparing model performance, on the training
data alone. [The leakage page](information-leakage.qmd) draws the line more carefully.
:::

## Where this breaks down

**Summary statistics hide what plots reveal.** A mean salinity of 33.9 after removing
sentinels looks fine, and conceals that one vessel's values are systematically high.
Plot by group.

**Some errors are undetectable.** Of the twelve depths recorded ten times too deep, ten
are obvious. Two — 125 m and 166 m — sit comfortably inside the plausible range and no
amount of looking will find them. Cleaning reduces error; it does not eliminate it.

**Automated profiling is a starting point, not an audit.** `skimr::skim()` and
`naniar::vis_miss()` will show you the missingness and the ranges in one call, and
neither will tell you that 1581 m is impossible *on this shelf*. That judgement is
yours.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- Exploratory analysis is damage assessment. Its output is a list of decisions, not a
  set of figures for the paper.
- Print the range of every numeric column and read it as a scientist. Sentinel values
  and decimal errors surface immediately.
- Count every level of every category. Twelve spellings of four substrates is normal,
  not exceptional.
- Ask whether missingness is patterned. Missing-in-winter is a different problem from
  missing-at-random, and only the first one biases results.
- Summarise by vessel, observer, year and gear. This is where instrument drift hides.
- Some errors are simply undetectable. Cleaning improves data; it does not sterilise it.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Run `naniar::vis_miss(raw)` and `skimr::skim(raw)`. What do they surface faster than
   the code above, and what do they miss entirely?
2. Take the depth values above 250 m. Divide them by ten. Do the corrected values fit
   the depth–temperature relationship of the rest of the survey? That is the kind of
   evidence that turns a guess about an error into a defensible correction.
